KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Model guidance is finally starting to hone in on some sort of 
agreement on the general nor'easter evolution. Very similar 
tracks and clusters are noted across GEFS, ECMWF Ens, and GEPS. 
The loop is now occurring closer to Long Island and thus the 
local impacts are somewhat capped by distance. However there 
really is not much change in the messaging that is necessary. We
still expect the same impacts and similar timing, it is the 
magnitude that is becoming a little more clear.

High surf: Available guidance is in solid agreement with seas 
peaking around 15 ft in the vicinity of Jeffrey's Ledge during 
the day Sat. Given the long duration northeast winds and 
favorable long fetch plus wind gusts perhaps approaching storm 
force I could see those significant wave heights reaching 18 ft 
or so. High Surf Advisory remains in effect for both large, 
breaking nearshore waves and high rip current risk. Those wave 
heights will likely remain at or above 10 ft into Sun.

Coastal flooding: A common theme of some of notable coastal 
flooding events has been prolonged surge over several tide 
cycles due to either slow or stalled storms. This one fits the 
bill for one that should be able to drive surge up to around 2 
ft. Guidance is a little lower than that, so we may need to bump
the surge forecasts up in the coming 24 hours. The track is 
actually a close match for the March 2018 nor'easter which 
brought several days of coastal flooding. Now the difference is 
that storm was much stronger and astronomical tides were about a
foot higher than those this weekend. The coastal flood forecast
matrix for the beaches south of Portland puts us right on the 
edge of Advisory and Warning. A Coastal Flood Watch has been 
issued for those areas given that we are on edge and 
preparations will need to be underway soon if action needs to be
taken.

Winds: Guidance is now providing some good confidence that the 
strongest winds will be Sat into Sat night. This is when the 
northeast LLJ is forecast to be the strongest, but we cannot 
quite match the magnitude forecast over southern New England. I 
have fairly high confidence that a 48+ hour period of greater 
than 30 kt gusts is likely. There is a window late Sat into Sun 
when we may mix down some slightly higher gusts. Either way 
leafed trees stressed by drought conditions and soaking rainfall
may combine to make tree damage a little more likely than 
usual. I still think a Wind Advisory is possible for portions of
southwestern Maine and southeastern NH. We still have some lead
time on that, but will likely need to make a decision by this 
afternoon.

Rainfall: This remains the lowest confidence impact of the 
bunch. Despite the growing confidence in track, guidance is 
still has a fair bit of spread on rainfall amounts and locations
of the heaviest QPF. There has been a trend to slow down the 
rainfall into the local area, with guidance not bringing a high 
likelihood of the first measurable precip until late Sat in some
cases. In addition the probability of 4 inches or more QPF has 
come down to 10 percent or less. Only the ECMWF Ens now has any 
threat of 2 inches QPF in 24 hrs, and that has shifted into late
Sun into Mon. So overall I do not anticipate flooding to be a 
concern from rainfall alone - there could be some drainage 
issues around high tides in the low lying areas. The best 
chances for 1 to 2 inches of rain will be southern NH into 
southwestern Maine, and the soaking rainfall is most likely 
south of the mtns. The biggest change with this forecast cycle 
is likely going to be extending the chances of rain thru Mon for
most locations.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

Strong high pressure and very dry air across northern New 
England will keep conditions dry through today. Moisture does 
begin to increase tonight with some showers possible, mainly 
across southern zones. 

Northeast winds will pick up today with gusts around 20-25 mph 
and perhaps 25-35 mph closer to the seacoast. 

Friday will also see deteriorating marine and surf conditions 
that will remain dangerous and all the way through the weekend.
